extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public, patrons of taste, artists/composers, and tradesmen
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive remarks on taste and appropriate practice across monuments/epitaphs, shop signs, music/opera, and genteel social conventions; aimed at improving public displays and artistic practice to suit national genius and public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monuments should represent the person's true character and achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments and inscriptions ought to celebrate the real distinguishing character and remarkable actions of the dead, not misrepresent them by ornamental fashion or by noting only the manner of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Sir Cloudesly Shovel's monument showing him as a beau in a long periwig and velvet cushions—this misrepresents the 'plain gallant Man.' The inscription that only records manner of death is inadequate because 'it was impossible for him to reap any Honour' from it. Prefer representations and inscriptions that reflect the person's deeds (e.g., naval rostra for admirals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit public monuments/inscriptions to men of learning before execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Public monuments and inscriptions should be reviewed by men of learning and genius before they are put in execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: A foreigner forms an idea of a nation's ignorance or politeness from public monuments; hence inscriptions should be elegant and just in thought and expression. Example: several modern epitaphs written with elegance do honour to living and dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extravagant or excessively modest epitaphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitaphs should neither be extravagantly flattering (which would embarrass the dead) nor so modest/obscure (e.g., in Greek or Hebrew) that they are not understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extravagant praise is a satyr on the departed; excessively modest inscriptions in languages few read render the monument meaningless to the public — 'not understood once in a Twelve-month.' Balance dignity and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate symbolic ornamentation for profession (authentic iconography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emblems and ornament on a monument should correspond to the person's profession and character (e.g., naval ornaments for admirals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: Dutch monuments of admirals adorned with rostral crowns, seaweed, shells, and coral that represent their naval service. Avoid generic or incongruous ornament that disguises true identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop signs should have affinity to the wares or trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Every shop should use a sign which bears some affinity to the wares in which it deals; signs should indicate trade or goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: a 'Bawd at the Sign of the Angel', a 'Taylor at the Lion', a goat before a perfumer, the French King's Head at a sword-cutler's. Recommendation: tradesmen should show marks of their trade before their doors; such marks help honest identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jarring or incongruous combinations on signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not join creatures or devices of jarring and incongruous natures together on the same sign (e.g., Bell and Neats-tongue, Dog and Gridiron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: flying pigs, hogs in armour, Fox and Seven Stars, Lamb and Dolphin together. Allowances: certain conceits (Cat and Fiddle) may be permissible if obviously witty; generally strive for coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish rules for quartering or borrowing another's sign
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be determinate rules for when a tradesman may 'give' or quarter the sign of another (e.g., a young tradesman adding his master's sign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: this practice has produced absurdities such as 'the three Nuns and a Hare.' Recommendation: limit and regulate quartering to prevent nonsensical combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use name-based/deviced signs to identify proprietor
rubrics_metrics.description: When a name suggests an ingenious device (visual pun), the owner may use that device to let the world know who he/she is (e.g., Mrs Salmon at the Trout, Mr Bell using a bell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefit: such signs can be witty and informative; historical examples: Abel Drugger's successful device, the Bell-Savage (philological origin 'la belle Sauvage'). These devices often invite popular wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs reveal inhabitant's humour/temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: One can often 'give a shrewd Guess at the Humour of the Inhabitant by the Sign that hangs before his Door' (e.g., a surly cholerick fellow chooses a Bear; milder dispositions choose a Lamb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation useful for social reading of the city; not a strict rule but a diagnostic heuristic when assessing public signage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitative/music must fit the accent and tone of the language
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitative music should be adapted to the tone or accent of the language it accompanies; one should not slavishly import Italian recitative into English with English words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems: using Italian recitative with English words yields mismatches where cadences signal anger or question in Italian but read as different passions in English—audiences misinterpret stage action. Recommendation: English composers should make gentle deviations from Italian recitative, borrowing graces but shaping cadences to the native accent and conversational tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit music (and arts) to the genius and taste of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: A composer (and by extension other artists) should fit his music to the genius of the people; art should accommodate national pronunciation, accent, and formed taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Lully cultivated French music with Italian graces to suit French ears. 'Let the Infusion be as strong as you please, but still let the Subject Matter of it be English.' Broad principle: the art adapts to taste, not vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts derive their laws from general sense and taste of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Music, architecture, painting, poetry, and oratory are to deduce their laws and rules from the general sense and taste of mankind, rather than impose art's principles on public taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: artists should test whether sounds/works genuinely express passion to ordinary ears; 'A Man of an ordinary Ear is a Judge whether a Passion is express'd in proper Sounds.' Avoid creating art pleasing only to specialized or 'chromatic' ears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage costuming/staging should not be ludicrously anachronistic or absurd
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage presentation (costume, properties) should suit the subject matter and not indulge in polite follies that make characters absurd (e.g., shepherds embroidered and wearing full-bottomed periwigs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: rivers in red stockings, Alpheus in a periwig, Pluto in French equipage with a valet de chambre — all are examples of folly and impertinence in staging. Keep costume and staging congruent with the story's nature and local taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club social rules as measures of propriety (Amorous Club example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A society of lovers (Amorous Club) is governed by rules meant to cultivate a particular mode of behaviour: admission requires a mistress and a poem; no disrespect to women; presidentship awarded by dignity of passion; expressive theatricality is valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural standard for that social institution: 'Without [a poem] no one can be admitted; for he that is not in love enough to rhyme, is unqualified.' The club forbids speaking disrespectfully of any woman (expulsion), counts sighing as required decorum, and settles rivalries by toasts and ritual (e.g., naevia sex cyathis...).
